title: Invariance under Gaussian null changes
statement: Let $n\ge 0$, and let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be measurable. If $A$ and $B$ agree almost everywhere with respect to standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^n$, then their Gaussian surface areas are equal.
hypotheses_covered: $A$ and $B$ agree almost everywhere for standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^n$
replaced: Let $n\ge0$, let $\gamma_n$ be standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^n$, and let $G,G\prime$ be independent vectors with law $\gamma_n$. Write $s_A(t)$ for the real value of the product-measure mass $(\gamma_n\otimes\gamma_n)\{(g,h):\mathbf1_A(g)\ne\mathbf1_A(\cos t\,g+\sin t\,h)\}$. Write $P_\gamma(A)=\liminf_{t\to0^+}\bigl[\sqrt{\pi/2}\,s_A(t)/t\bigr]_+$ in $[0,\infty]$, where $[x]_+=\max(x,0)$. If measurable sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ agree almost everywhere under $\gamma_n$, then $P_\gamma(A)=P_\gamma(B)$.
